b: He was born Andras Istvan Grof in Budapest on the second of September 1936. His father ran a small dairy business. By the time the boy was four, scarlet fever had very nearly killed him and had taken a good deal of his hearing, and for the rest of his life he would watch mouths move and fill in the gaps by reasoning. A useful thing to know about a man who built a career on faint signals.

When he was eight the Germans occupied Hungary. His father was taken to a labour battalion. Andras and his mother obtained forged papers, took Christian names that were not theirs, and were hidden by acquaintances while the city was bombed and then besieged. His father came back after the war, beaten and worked almost to death, so altered that the boy did not at first know him. They had survived by being quick, quiet and willing to become somebody else.

This is the first thing worth understanding about the book he wrote fifty years later. Grove did not reach the idea that the ground can move under a going concern by reading a case study. He had watched a city, a currency and an entire set of rules about who was permitted to exist all change inside a few months. Then the Communists arrived, the dairy was nationalised, and it happened again.

b: In October 1956 Hungary rose against its Soviet backed government. Grove was twenty and studying chemistry in Budapest. When the tanks returned in November and the rising was crushed, he decided with very little deliberation to leave. He crossed on foot into Austria with a group of strangers, guided through marshland by a man who knew the way, and from Vienna reached the United States by ship early in 1957 with almost no money and very little English.

He enrolled at the City College of New York, then free, and chose chemical engineering because it paid. He could not reliably hear a lecture, so he borrowed notes, read the textbook ahead of the class, and worked out from the equations what the lecturer must have said. He graduated first in his year in 1960. His memoir of those years stops at the moment he lands in America.

It matters because he had already done, in his own life, the thing his book would later ask of companies. He had seen that his old position was finished, accepted a stretch of being nobody in particular, and come out in an occupation he had not previously had. He knew from the inside how frightening the middle of that passage is.

b: He took a doctorate in chemical engineering at Berkeley, finishing in 1963, and went straight to Fairchild Semiconductor, the firm that was then inventing the modern chip industry. He worked in the research laboratory under Gordon Moore on the physics of the silicon surface, the thin and badly behaved boundary where a transistor actually does its work. Nobody fully understood it. Devices drifted and failed for reasons that were put down to bad luck.

Grove's contribution was to insist that the drift had causes and that the causes could be measured. He and his colleagues traced instability to mobile contamination in the oxide layer and to charge trapped at the interface, and that knowledge made reliable metal oxide devices possible. In 1967 he published a textbook on semiconductor devices which was used for a generation.

The habit formed here never left him. If a thing matters, find a number for it, then argue about what the number means rather than about whose impression is stronger. He would apply that same procedure to a dying business, and later to his own illness.

b: When Moore and Robert Noyce left Fairchild in the summer of 1968 to start Intel, Grove went with them. He joined on the day the company was incorporated, as its third employee and its director of engineering. He was careful, all his life, to say that he was not a founder. He was the man who made the thing run.

The business was memory. Intel's 1103 dynamic memory chip, shipped in 1970, became the best selling semiconductor in the world and built the company. Memory was more than a product line. It was where the hardest manufacturing problems were solved first, so to be an Intel person was to be a memory person. Microprocessors, invented there in 1971, were for years a curiosity sold to makers of cash registers.

In 1983 Grove published a book about management, and it is worth knowing what is in it, because it is the machine the later book takes apart. A manager's output, he argued, is the output of his own organisation plus that of the neighbouring organisations he influences, and nothing else. So find the few activities with the highest leverage and spend your time there. Meetings are not an interruption of managerial work but the medium of it. Training your people returns more than anything else you can do.
He had written down, in other words, how to run a well aimed company. The second book is about what happens when a well run company is aimed at the wrong thing.

b: In 1979 Intel began losing design contests. Motorola's new processor was the one engineers wanted, and Intel's salespeople were coming back empty handed. One of them, a field engineer called Don Buckout, wrote a long and alarmed report about what he was meeting in customers' offices. His manager forwarded it upwards rather than filing it, and it reached Grove.

Grove's response was not to doubt the salesman. In December 1979 he pulled a task force together and gave it a week. The plan it produced was called Operation Crush, and its insight was that Intel could not win on the specification sheet, so it should stop competing there. It would sell the whole package instead, the development tools, the support, the roadmap of future parts, the promise that a customer who designed in an Intel chip would be looked after for a decade. The target was two thousand design wins in a year.

They got them. One, taken by a salesman in Boca Raton in Florida, was a secretive project at a large office machine company, and in August 1981 it was announced as the IBM Personal Computer, with an Intel processor inside. Nobody understood at the time that this single win would matter more than the other nineteen hundred and ninety nine together.

Two lessons were banked. An urgent, named, resourced response to a threat can work. And the warning had come from the lowest paid man in the chain, so the company was saved because somebody passed it on.

b: Then came the thing the book exists to describe. Japanese manufacturers had spent the late nineteen seventies learning to make memory chips with better yields, tighter quality and far more capital behind them, and in 1984 all that capacity arrived at once. Orders that had been booked solid stopped in the autumn. Prices fell through the floor and kept going. Intel's memory business, the heart and the self image of the company, began losing very large sums with no prospect of a turn.

Grove's word for what had arrived is a ten times force. Somewhere around a business sit six pressures, and he was explicit about them. Existing competitors. Suppliers. Customers. Potential competitors. Complementors, meaning the firms whose products make yours worth having. And the possibility that what you sell could be delivered in an altogether different way. When any one of those grows roughly ten times stronger, the rules by which you have been making money stop holding, and no amount of working harder inside the old rules will help. That is a strategic inflection point. The deadliest of the six, he insisted, is the last one, substitution, because it does not arrive as a rival doing your job better but as somebody making your job unnecessary.

The trouble is that at the time you cannot tell. A ten times force and an ordinary downturn look identical for a year or more, and the data arrives too late to settle the argument. Intel spent eighteen months in meetings. Build a dedicated memory plant. Find a technology leap. Wait for the cycle. Grove named that condition strategic dissonance, the state in which what senior management says the company is doing has come apart from what it is doing.

b: In the middle of 1985, worn down by the argument, Grove asked Gordon Moore a question that has since been repeated in every management course in the world. If we got kicked out and the board brought in a new chief executive, what do you think he would do? Moore answered without hesitating that he would get the company out of memories. Then Grove said the line that made the book. Why should the two of us not walk out of the door, come back in, and do it ourselves.

He had performed a small trick on himself. The obstacle was never the data. It was that the men holding the data had built their lives on the business the data condemned. By imagining himself sacked that morning and rehired that afternoon, he was left with the decision alone.

And then he found something that unsettled him more than the loss. The production planners had a quiet rule for allocating scarce factory capacity. They gave it to whichever product earned the most margin on a wafer. Memory earned almost nothing, microprocessors a great deal. Month by month, with nobody deciding anything and no announcement of any kind, those planners had already moved most of Intel out of memory, a year or more before its chief executive could say so.

From this came his least comfortable conclusion. Strategic actions precede strategic plans. The people in contact with the market adjust first, because they must, while those at the top are insulated by layers of good news and by the memory of how the money used to be made. If you want to know your real strategy, read where the capacity is going, not the plan.

The exit was announced in October 1985 and took about three years to finish. More than seven thousand people lost their jobs. And Grove admitted that for roughly a year afterwards he could not bring himself to stand before the sales force and say the plain sentence, that Intel was now a microprocessor company.

b: Out of the wreckage came the bet. Intel's new thirty two bit processor was ready in 1985. Industry convention said a big customer would not design in a chip with only one maker, so you licensed a rival to make it too. Intel decided to be the only source, and to build enough capacity that no customer need be frightened.

The large established customer hesitated, preferring the older part it already controlled. A much smaller Texas firm did not, and in September 1986 it shipped the first personal computer built on the new chip. The market followed the smaller firm. Intel held both the design and the only factory, and kept the margins of that position for fifteen years. Everything Intel later became dates from those two decisions, the retreat and the bet, taken within a year of each other.

Grove's description of how to behave during such a passage is the most practical thing in the book. Let chaos reign, then rein in chaos. While you genuinely do not know which way the world has turned, fund the experiments that contradict the official plan, including the ones run by people arguing with you. Then stop, choose, say it plainly, and move the money behind the choice with a force that feels excessive.

Most organisations manage only one half. They either suppress the awkward experiments and reach clarity too late, or they debate for ever and never commit, which Grove called wandering in the valley of death. The valley is the crossing itself, when the old business no longer pays and the new one does not yet.

b: Nine years later it happened again, and he got it wrong first. On the thirteenth of June 1994 a mathematics lecturer at a small college in Virginia, Thomas Nicely, noticed that sums involving prime numbers came out inconsistently on his new machine. He spent four months eliminating every other explanation, his own code, the board, the compiler. On the nineteenth of October he was satisfied the processor itself was wrong, and on the twenty fourth he told Intel. Hearing nothing useful, on the thirtieth he wrote to academic colleagues asking them to test their own machines.

The flaw was tiny and real. The division circuit used a lookup table, and five entries that should have held a particular value held zero instead, lost when the fabrication masks were made. Certain divisions came back very slightly wrong. Intel had found the error itself by June, corrected it in new production, and calculated that an ordinary spreadsheet user would meet it perhaps once in tens of thousands of years. On the engineering merits, defensible.

It was also the wrong answer, and the reason is the whole point. The trade press carried the story on the seventh of November, a television news segment on the twenty second put it before the public, and in December the biggest computer maker in the world stopped shipping machines containing the chip. Intel spent six weeks explaining statistics to people who were not asking about statistics. On the twentieth of December it gave up and offered to replace any affected processor on request, and in January 1995 took a charge of four hundred and seventy five million dollars.

Grove's reading of his own mistake is the finest passage in the book. A ten times force had hit him and he had answered it with the old rules. Intel had spent three years and a fortune putting its name on the outside of other people's computers, and had thereby stopped being an anonymous components supplier whose customers were purchasing managers and become a consumer brand answerable to the public. A components supplier may tell a customer that a defect is statistically negligible. A consumer brand may not tell a man that his arithmetic is probably fine.

Note also where the warning came from. Not the sales force this time but outside the company altogether, through a channel no procedure covered, from a man with no commercial standing at all. Grove's instruction is to hunt for such people, call them your Cassandras, and listen longest to the ones whose news you least want.

b: In 1995, while writing the book, Grove was told he had prostate cancer. He did what he had done to the silicon surface thirty years before. He read the primary literature himself, built his own charts comparing the published outcomes of the competing treatments, noticed that each specialist recommended the procedure he personally performed, and chose a course his urologist had not advised. Then he published the whole analysis, charts included, in a business magazine in 1996.

That is the last move of the book. Its final chapter argues that a career is a business with a single employee, and that you are both its workforce and its chief executive. The same six forces press on you. Your skill can be substituted, your employer can become a weaker complement than it was, your industry can take a ten times force while your performance reviews stay excellent. So ask whether the thing you are paid for is becoming easier to get elsewhere, and move while you still have a choice rather than when the choice is made for you. Fear, he says plainly, is useful. Complacency breeds failure, and only the paranoid survive.

He stepped down as chief executive in 1998 and as chairman in 2004, was told in 2000 that he had Parkinson's disease, spoke about it openly and paid for a great deal of research into it, and died at his home in Los Altos in California on the twenty first of March 2016, aged seventy nine.

The honest ending is this. The company that wrote the manual then walked into its own inflection point and missed it. Intel declined to build the processor for the first smartphone that mattered, spent a decade losing the mobile market, and by the twenty twenties had handed manufacturing leadership to a Taiwanese contract maker it once out engineered. Critics add, fairly, that an inflection point is far easier to name afterwards than to spot at the time. That does not weaken the method. It shows how hard the method is to use on yourself, which is exactly why Grove had to invent a trick to fire himself before he could do it.

ch.h: You Are Your Own Chief Executive

note: Dates and events come from Grove's own books, his memoir of his Hungarian years, Intel company history and contemporary reporting of the 1985 memory exit and the 1994 processor recall. The exchange with Gordon Moore about a new chief executive is Grove's own retelling and its exact wording varies slightly between accounts, so it is given here in substance. The number of job losses in the memory exit is an approximation drawn from Intel's headcount over 1985 to 1987. The claim that Intel later missed the mobile transition is widely argued rather than settled, though Intel's own former chief executive publicly confirmed declining the first iPhone processor.
recall: What ten times force hit Intel in 1984, and what did Grove and Moore conclude in mid 1985?

Japanese manufacturers flooded the market with better and cheaper memory chips, and Intel's memory business collapsed into heavy losses. In mid 1985 Grove asked Moore what a newly hired chief executive would do, and Moore said he would get Intel out of memories. They decided to act as though they were that new management, and the exit was announced in October 1985.
Who had already begun moving Intel out of memory before the executives decided, and by what mechanism?

The production planners had done it. They allocated scarce factory capacity to whichever product earned the most margin per wafer, which meant microprocessors rather than memory. Month by month, with no decision taken and nothing announced, they had shifted most of the company before the leadership could say so.
Name the six forces Grove watches, and say which he considers most dangerous.

Existing competitors, suppliers, customers, potential competitors, complementors, and the possibility that your product could be built in a completely different way. The last one, substitution, is the deadliest, because it does not beat you at your own job but removes the need for the job.
Who found the Pentium division flaw, and what did Intel do on the twentieth of December 1994?

Thomas Nicely, a mathematics lecturer at a small Virginia college, noticed inconsistent prime number calculations in June 1994 and reported the processor flaw to Intel that October. After press and television coverage and a halt in shipments by a major computer maker, Intel offered on the twentieth of December to replace any affected chip on request, taking a charge of four hundred and seventy five million dollars the following January.
What was Operation Crush, and which design win made it historically important?

It was the urgent campaign Grove launched in December 1979 after a field engineer warned that Intel was losing design contests to Motorola. Intel stopped competing on specifications and sold the whole package of tools, support and roadmap instead, aiming for two thousand design wins in a year. One of them, won in Florida, became the IBM Personal Computer announced in August 1981.
take: Name the force before arguing tactics
When returns stop responding to effort, work out which of the six pressures has grown about ten times stronger. Arguments about tactics are wasted until everyone agrees what has changed.
Substitution is the one that kills
Rivals doing your job better are survivable. Somebody making your job unnecessary is not. Ask regularly how a stranger could deliver what you sell by an entirely different route.
Find your Cassandras and keep them
Bad news reaches the edge of an organisation first, in sales, support and the field. Ask those people directly, write down what they say, and give the most weight to the news you least enjoy.
Read the budget, not the plan
Your real strategy is where capacity, cash and good people are actually going this month. Follow the allocation and you will see the decision long before anyone announces it.
When you are too invested to think clearly, ask what a successor with no history here would do on their first morning. Then do that, since you are allowed to be your own successor.
Let chaos reign, then rein in chaos

While genuinely unsure, fund the experiments that contradict your plan, including your critics' ones. Then stop the debate, state the new direction, and move resources behind it harder than feels comfortable.
Say the new sentence out loud
A change is not complete until you can state the new identity in one plain sentence and repeat it until the front line uses it unprompted. Grove needed a year to manage this.
Run your career as a business of one
Watch the forces acting on your own trade, not just your performance reviews. Build the skill the market is starting to want while you still have the choice of when to move.
title: The Man Who Fired Himself
wiifm: You already know that markets shift. What you do not know is how to tell an ordinary bad quarter from the change that quietly ends your business, or what to do in the long months when you cannot yet tell the difference. Andy Grove took Intel through two of those moments and then wrote down the mechanics. By the end of this you will know what a strategic inflection point is, which of six competitive forces to watch, why your own staff will have worked out the answer before you do, and why the clearest warning you ever receive will come from somebody you are inclined to ignore.
